issue_context.title: API server creates one etcd client per CRD
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

Currently the API server is creating one etcd client per CRD. This causes it to use more memory and more TCP connections than it should need to. In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111477 we significantly reduced the amount of memory said clients use by updating them to share a single logger, but we should address the underlying issue.

I've heard various folks, including @aojea and @lavalamp mention that they've looked into addressing this but I couldn't immediately find a tracking issue. We were previously discussing this in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111476 which was closed by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111477, but there seems to be agreement that the "correct fix" is what is tracked by this issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Presuming that a single etcd client can handle multiple requests at once, I'd expect the API server to use approximately one etcd client (i.e. one https://pkg.go.dev/go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3#Client) per etcd cluster it's connected to. I say approximately because I see that additional clients are also used for things like health probes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a kind cluster and deploy a few CRDs. 

```console
$ k get crd|wc -l
1878

# Enter the kind cluster's control plane container.
$ docker exec -it e092b6d27bf-withlogger-control-plane bash

# Find the API server's PID
root@e092b6d27bf-withlogger-control-plane:/# ps -C kube-apiserver
    PID TTY          TIME CMD
    493 ?        00:29:03 kube-apiserver

# Count how many etcd connections exist with the 1,878 CRDs loaded
# Column 3 is the remote host and port per https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/networking/proc_net_tcp.txt
# 0100007F:094B is hex for 127.0.0.1:2379 (the etcd client port)
root@e092b6d27bf-withlogger-control-plane:/# cat /proc/493/net/tcp|awk '{ print $3 }'|grep '0100007F:094B'|wc -l
1937

# Back outside of the kind control plane container, delete all your CRDs
$ k delete crds --all

# Then back inside the container re-count the connections
root@e092b6d27bf-withlogger-control-plane:/# cat /proc/493/net/tcp|awk '{ print $3 }'|grep '0100007F:094B'|wc -l
60
```

Note that 1,937 - 60 = 1,877 - the number of CRDs we have loaded (the 1,878 above includes the header line).

### Anything else we need to know?

Based on my read of the code, I see roughly:

* All of /apis is handled by a *crdHandler
* When a request comes in it gets an instance of the crd (from an informer)
* Gets serving info from a map of CRDs - if there is none it...
* Calls customresource.NewStorage which creates a genericregistry.Store
* Calls its CompleteWithOptions method
* That calls its “Decorator”, which is a genericregistry.StorageWithCacher
* That calls generic.NewRawStorage which just wraps factory.Create
* factory.Create calls newETCD3Storage which calls newETCD3Client

Merging clients, as @aojea suggests, would increase the blast radius.  We've already experienced issues with overloaded gRPC/etcd clients impacting other requests.  For example, [etcd#15402](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15402) demonstrates how LIST operations can starve WATCH requests, and [kubernetes#123448](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123448) illustrates how direct etcd WATCH requests can starve the watch cache.

Furthermore, the ConsistentReadsFromCache mechanism relies on separate WATCH streams.  It sends progress notification requests to etcd, which only respond when all WATCH requests within a stream are synchronized. Combining clients would allow a single overloaded CRD to prevent progress notifications for other resources.

While separating CRDs keeps us well below any connection breaking point, blindly combining connections risks easily exceeding that limit. This could lead to difficult-to-debug issues.  Therefore, I don't think we should proceed with connection consolidation until we understand and are ready to tackle those breaking points.

nit: this part of the comment has utility only in the scope of this PR - after that point nobody will remember the previous state. might re-word as:

> capturing this state with a closure ... makes it possible to write tests to [validate what, exactly?] without having to actually start etcd connections

Is this 100% safe? For the kube-apiserver I can't think of any actual problems, but this staging repo allows anyone to write a binary that starts an API server, this appears to leak a client in that case..

This `client` always comes from `newETCD3Client` which always comes from `TransportConfig.Client` which is always lifecycled with the `ctx` passed into `TransportConfig.Complete`.  Since the fields are private, it is impossible to get a client without calling `Complete` meaning any custom code that calls into this function would be at fault if it chose to pass in something like `context.TODO()`.  The standard wiring used by aggregated API servers always passes in a valid context.  Is there some other leak that you are seeing?

Not sure if this would be acceptable or not, but if this is going to be a process-ending error anyway (right?), could panic here and not require the error propagation changes up the stack.

Almost all of the config construction code eventually leads to a fatal error.  There are a few places where we use `klog.Fatal` but I would really prefer to avoid that - this only has two non-test callers so the error propagation is minimal IMO.
